text:
The primary material of a candle is, of course, wax. But let us not be so pedestrian as to think of it merely as paraffin or soy. In the grand theater of adulthood, the candle is the true protagonist of our nightly rituals, standing tall and stoic while we, the weary protagonists of this tragicomedy, collapse onto the couch.

Its purpose? To provide a flickering, amber glow that illuminates the stark reality of our existence: that "spontaneity" is now just a fancy word for choosing between chicken and beef instant noodles, and "long-term planning" is a high-stakes debate over whether to rewatch *The Office* for the forty-seventh time or finally start that show everyone is talking about.

The candle burns down, inch by inch, mirroring the slow, inexorable drain of our energy as we calculate the exact cost of electricity versus the joy of not turning on the main light. It is a beacon of hope in a world where the most exciting part of the day is realizing you have enough money to pay the electric bill that powers the candle. It is a silent witness to our back pain, our Netflix paralysis, and our profound, existential dread masked as a casual dinner choice. Truly, the wax is not just wax; it is the solidified form of our lost youth, melting away one evening at a time.
